## Introduction

Digital music collections have expanded rapidly in recent decades, and the recent market shift away from purchase of individual albums towards subscriptions to streaming platforms has significantly changed the way we listen to music (Wlomert et al., 2025). Streaming platforms like Spotify and Apple Music hold tens of millions of songs that can quickly become overwhelming for listeners exploring new music (Spotify ‘For the Record’, 2026; Apple Newsroom Release, 2022; Wlomert et al., 2025). Consequently, classification of defining song characteristics such as genre is increasingly useful for suggesting related songs, and building customized, genre-specific playlists. 

Music information retrieval (MIR) is an active area of research, and music genre classification has been identified as a challenging task given the diversity of audio features and the subjective, dynamic definitions of unique genres (Ramirez and Flores, 2020). Previous work on music genre classification has employed several machine learning algorithms, including Support Vector Machines (SVMs), k-Nearest-Neighbour (k-NN) classification algorithms, and has more recently involved advanced deep learning techniques (Narkhede et al., 2022; Ramirez and Flores, 2020). Here, we investigate the effectiveness of a k-NN model and ask whether a k-NN model can predict a candidate genre for songs based on various song features. We selected a k-NN model based on its simplicity and interpretability for predicting the genre of future related songs.

In our study, we use Spotify song data (R for Data Science Online Learning Community, 2020) collected from the Spotify Web API using the spotifyr package (Thompson et al., 2024). This data set contains total 28,356 unique songs, each with twelve numeric audio descriptive features. These features include:

    1. danceability (scale of 0-1, based on a combination of musical elements); 
    2. energy (scale of 0-1, based on measure of intensity and activity); 
    3. key (ordinal integer based on standard pitch Class notation that measures the estimated overall key of the track);
    4. loudness (measures the overall loudness of the track in decibels, dB); 
    5. mode (indicates the modality if song is in major (1) or minor (0)); 
    6. speechiness (a measure of the presence of spoken words in a song, ranging from 0-1); 
    7. acousticness (a confidence level of whether the track is acoustic, ranging from 0-1); 
    8. instrumentalness (measure of whether a track contains no vocals, ranging from 0-1); 
    9. liveness (measure of the presence of a live audience in the song recording, ranging from 0-1); 
    10. valence (measure describing the musical positiveness conveyed by the song, ranging from 0-1); 
    11. tempo (estimated tempo of the song in beats per minute, bpm); and 
    12. duration (duration of the song in milliseconds, ms). 

The target we aim to predict is a candidate playlist genre for the song, one of EDM, latin, pop, R&B, rap and rock, determined from existing user-created and Spotify playlists that contain these songs.

## Methods

We used a K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifier to predict a song's playlist genre based on its audio features. KNN works by identifying songs with similar feature values and using their genres to make a prediction, making it a suitable approach for exploring whether songs with similar audio characteristics tend to belong to the same genre. Rather than learning a fixed relationship between each feature and genre, the model relies on similarities between songs, which aligns with our question of whether audio features can help distinguish musical genres.

We evaluated the model using accuracy, which represents the proportion of songs correctly classified out of all predictions. We chose accuracy because it provides an intuitive measure of the model's overall performance across the genre categories. To determine the best-performing configuration, we used cross-validation on the training data to compare different feature subsets and values of k, then selected the combination with the highest mean cross-validation accuracy. Finally, we evaluated the selected model on the held-out test set to assess how well it generalized to unseen songs.

### Data download and cleaning

We downloaded the Spotify Songs dataset from TidyTuesday. Because each row represents a single playlist entry, songs that appear on multiple playlists are listed more than once.

```{python}
DATA_URL = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/"
    "data/2020/2020-01-21/spotify_songs.csv"
)
RAW_DIR = Path("../data/raw")
PROCESSED_DIR = Path("../data/processed")
RAW_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
PROCESSED_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

raw_path = RAW_DIR / "spotify_songs.csv"
response = requests.get(DATA_URL, timeout=60)
response.raise_for_status()
raw_path.write_bytes(response.content)

spotify_raw = pd.read_csv(raw_path)
spotify_raw.shape
```

To prepare and clean the dataset, we kept only the columns needed for modelling: each song’s ID, title, artist, playlist genre (our target), and Spotify’s twelve numeric audio features (such as energy and tempo). Duplicate entries could put the same song in both the training and test sets and make a test score look better than it is. To prevent data leakage of this sort, we retain only the first occurrence of each song.


```{python}
FEATURES = [
    "danceability",
    "energy",
    "key",
    "loudness",
    "mode",
    "speechiness",
    "acousticness",
    "instrumentalness",
    "liveness",
    "valence",
    "tempo",
    "duration_ms",
]
TARGET = "playlist_genre"

spotify_clean = (
    spotify_raw[["track_id", "track_name", "track_artist", TARGET] + FEATURES]
    .drop_duplicates(subset="track_id", keep="first")
    .dropna(subset=[TARGET] + FEATURES)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
spotify_clean.to_csv(PROCESSED_DIR / "spotify_songs_clean.csv", index=False)

print(f"Rows before cleaning: {len(spotify_raw):,}")
print(f"Rows after cleaning: {len(spotify_clean):,}")
```

### Train/test split

Before exploring the data or making any modelling decisions, we set aside 20% of the songs as a test set and kept the remaining 80% for training. We split the data so that each genre makes up the same share of both sets, and locked in the random split with a fixed seed (522) to make the process reproducible with the same test split. The test set will be untouched until we evaluate our final model.

```{python}
train_df, test_df = train_test_split(
    spotify_clean,
    test_size=0.2,
    stratify=spotify_clean[TARGET],
    random_state=522,
)
train_df.to_csv(PROCESSED_DIR / "spotify_train.csv", index=False)
test_df.to_csv(PROCESSED_DIR / "spotify_test.csv", index=False)

print(f"Training set: {len(train_df):,} songs")
print(f"Test set: {len(test_df):,} songs")
```

### Exploratory data analysis


#### Summary of Training Data

We explored the training set to understand the distribution of playlist genres and the audio features used for classification. Only training data was used to avoid influencing the analysis with information from the test set.

```{python}
from IPython.display import display

print(f"Training set: {train_df.shape[0]:,} songs")
print(f"Number of playlist genres: {train_df[TARGET].nunique()}")
print(f"Missing values: {train_df[FEATURES + [TARGET]].isna().sum().sum()}")
```

**Table 1. Distribution of playlist genres in the training set.**

```{python}
genre_summary = (
    train_df[TARGET]
    .value_counts()
    .rename_axis("Playlist genre")
    .reset_index(name="Number of songs")
)

genre_summary["Percentage (%)"] = (
    genre_summary["Number of songs"] / len(train_df) * 100
).round(1)

display(genre_summary)
```


Table 1 shows the distribution of songs across six playlist genres in the training set. Rap has the most songs (19.0%), while Latin has the fewest (14.6%). Overall, the genre distribution is relatively balanced, with no single genre dominating the dataset.


**Table 2. Descriptive statistics of continuous audio features in the training set.**

```{python}
continuous_features = [
    feature for feature in FEATURES
    if feature not in ["key", "mode"]
]

audio_data = train_df[continuous_features].copy()
audio_data["duration_ms"] = audio_data["duration_ms"] / 1000
audio_data = audio_data.rename(
    columns={"duration_ms": "duration (seconds)"}
)

feature_summary = (
    audio_data
    .agg(["mean", "std", "min", "max"])
    .T
    .rename(columns={
        "mean": "Mean",
        "std": "SD",
        "min": "Min",
        "max": "Max"
    })
    .rename_axis("Audio feature")
    .reset_index()
    .round(3)
)

display(feature_summary)
```


Table 2 summarizes the continuous audio features in the training set. Songs have an average danceability of 0.653, energy of 0.698, and tempo of approximately 121 BPM. The features have different measurement scales, especially tempo and duration compared to features ranging from 0 to 1. Therefore, feature scaling is important before applying KNN classification. Key and mode were excluded from this summary because they are discrete variables.





#### **Visualization of Training Data**

We created two visualizations using only the training data to explore the genre distribution and differences in audio features.

```{python}
#| label: fig-genre-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Number of songs in each playlist genre in the training set."

import altair as alt

genre_chart = (
    alt.Chart(genre_summary)
    .mark_bar()
    .encode(
        x=alt.X("Playlist genre:N", sort="-y", title="Playlist genre"),
        y=alt.Y("Number of songs:Q", title="Number of songs"),
        tooltip=["Playlist genre:N", "Number of songs:Q"]
    )
    .properties(
        width=600,
        height=350,
        title="Distribution of Playlist Genres"
    )
)

display(genre_chart)
```

@fig-genre-distribution shows the distribution of playlist genres in the training set. Rap has the most songs (4,321), while Latin has the fewest (3,310). Overall, the six genres are relatively balanced, with no single genre dominating the training set.

```{python}
#| label: fig-energy-by-genre
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of song energy across playlist genres in the training set."

alt.data_transformers.disable_max_rows()

energy_chart = (
    alt.Chart(train_df[[TARGET, "energy"]])
    .mark_boxplot()
    .encode(
        x=alt.X(
            "playlist_genre:N",
            title="Playlist genre",
            sort=genre_summary["Playlist genre"].tolist()
        ),
        y=alt.Y(
            "energy:Q",
            title="Energy (0–1)",
            scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 1])
        )
    )
    .properties(
        width=600,
        height=350,
        title="Energy Distribution by Playlist Genre"
    )
)

display(energy_chart)
```

@fig-energy-by-genre compares the energy distributions across the six playlist genres. EDM has the highest median energy, while R&B has the lowest. However, the distributions overlap across genres, suggesting that energy alone may not be enough to classify songs accurately. Combining multiple audio features may help improve KNN classification.



```{python}
#| label: fig-feature-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of continuous audio features in the training set."

import numpy as np

# Prepare the continuous audio features
plot_features = [f for f in FEATURES if f not in ["key", "mode"]]

plot_data = train_df[plot_features].copy()
plot_data["duration_ms"] = plot_data["duration_ms"] / 1000
plot_data = plot_data.rename(
    columns={"duration_ms": "duration (seconds)"}
)

# Calculate distribution frequencies for each feature
histogram_rows = []

for feature in plot_data.columns:
    values = plot_data[feature].dropna()
    counts, edges = np.histogram(values, bins=25)

    for i in range(len(counts)):
        histogram_rows.append({
            "feature": feature,
            "bin_center": (edges[i] + edges[i + 1]) / 2,
            "count": counts[i]
        })

histogram_df = pd.DataFrame(histogram_rows)

# Create individual area plots with independent axes
charts = []

for feature in plot_data.columns:
    feature_hist = histogram_df[
        histogram_df["feature"] == feature
    ]

    chart = (
        alt.Chart(feature_hist)
        .mark_area(opacity=0.7)
        .encode(
            x=alt.X("bin_center:Q", title="Feature value"),
            y=alt.Y("count:Q", title="Number of songs")
        )
        .properties(
            width=250,
            height=130,
            title=feature
        )
    )

    charts.append(chart)

# Arrange plots in 2 columns
rows = [
    alt.hconcat(charts[i], charts[i + 1])
    for i in range(0, len(charts), 2)
]

feature_chart = alt.vconcat(*rows)

display(feature_chart)
```


@fig-feature-distributions shows the distributions of the continuous audio features in the training set. Most songs have relatively high danceability and energy, while speechiness, acousticness, and instrumentalness are strongly right-skewed, with many values close to zero. Tempo is mostly concentrated around 100–150 BPM, and song duration is generally around 150–300 seconds. The features also have very different scales, highlighting the importance of feature scaling before KNN classification.
